This paper introduces a novel approach to robotic motor learning by utilizing a specific exploration strategy. The proposed method focuses on maximizing the variance of the robot's end-effector, thereby targeting states where the current policy exhibits high uncertainty. The resulting exploration-driven policy gradient algorithm is designed to be model-free, gradient-based, and capable of model-free, gradient-based learning. The method is evaluated on a high-dimensional, 7-DOF robotic arm tasked with reaching a target location. The findings demonstrate that the proposed strategy outperforms baseline methods by generating more effective motor learning. The source code is available at: https://github.com/robotics/robotics

This study examines the heat capacity of a classical particle in an anharmonic potential using the canonical ensemble. The analysis demonstrates that the heat capacity can be expressed via the renormalized frequency of small oscillations around the potential's minimum. Furthermore, the article establishes a correspondence between this renormalized frequency and the heat capacity within the harmonic approximation.

We examine two- and three-point correlation functions within the context of the Jackiw-Teitelboim model, specifically focusing on the non-unitary crosscap state. Our findings reveal that these correlators exhibit a distinct non-exponential decay at late times, a feature that stands in contrast to the behavior observed in unitary theories. Additionally, we demonstrate that these correlators adhere to the principles of the Schwarzian derivative and remain consistent with the underlying modular Hamiltonian.

The 2020 U.S. presidential election saw numerous social media platforms crack down on misinformation regarding the election and its outcome. This study examines Twitter's response to the election, specifically analyzing the reasons behind account suspensions. We investigate whether the reasons for suspensions were clearly communicated to users and whether the bans were applied fairly and consistently. By utilizing a dataset of 1,000 accounts that were suspended during the election, we examine the relationship between account characteristics and the justifications provided for their removal. We find that Twitter's enforcement policies disproportionately targeted accounts with a high level of political activity, suggesting a bias against political speech. Additionally, we observe that the explanations given for suspensions were often vague and did not adequately inform users of the specific rules they had violated.

The LHC is the world's premier particle accelerator, currently dedicated to high-energy proton-proton collisions. We introduce a proposal to adapt the LHC for an electron-hadron collider experiment. This setup would utilize the LHC's existing infrastructure to achieve center-of-mass energies of 1.4 TeV in electron-proton interactions, thereby extending the reach of the international electron-ion collider (EIC) by a factor of two. This proposed electron beam would originate from an independent circular accelerator, allowing for independent control of the electron and proton beams. This independent control offers significant advantages, such as the ability to probe the nucleus at extremely high momentum fractions ($x$) and to conduct deep inelastic scattering at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV.

Crowdsourcing has become a prevalent method for gathering data, yet it often results in inconsistent quality. This study introduces a novel framework designed to address noisy crowdsourced data, specifically for the task of identifying and filtering out unreliable contributors. The approach employs ensemble modeling combined with a custom "human softmax" distribution to quantify uncertainty. This distribution is derived by training a softmax neural network on a specific contributor's dataset and then calculating the entropy of the resulting output probabilities. The efficacy of this method was evaluated using two real-world datasets: one focused on medical image classification and another on sentiment analysis. The findings demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively distinguishes between high- and low-quality contributors, with the ensemble model and "human softmax" distribution proving superior to baseline methods.

This study introduces a multiple access strategy for distributed vehicle networks that adapts to environmental conditions. The primary objective is to maximize the average network throughput by dynamically selecting between grant-based and grant-free methods based on real-time channel states. We model this challenge as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and develop a corresponding Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms traditional grant-only and grant-only hybrid schemes in terms of throughput.

The past decade has seen the Deep Learning revolution transform Artificial Intelligence, driving unprecedented advancements in computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition. This paper offers a comprehensive review of these breakthroughs, along with their applications and the underlying technologies. It also explores the pivotal role of the ImageNet dataset in fostering the AI revolution and provides a holistic view of AI's current state and future prospects.

Software engineering research has increasingly focused on feature toggles, a technique that enables incremental development by allowing new features to be deployed independently of their corresponding backend code. This study investigates the impact of feature toggles on software quality and maintenance efforts within open-source environments. Specifically, we analyze how the adoption of these features influences merge conflicts, resolution times, and defect rates. Our analysis leveraged data from 11 open-source projects, examining 1,077 feature toggles alongside 1,077 related commits. Our findings indicate that feature toggles are positively correlated with reduced merge conflicts and faster resolution times. Additionally, we discovered a correlation between toggles and an increase in defect density. These results suggest that while feature toggles facilitate smoother integration processes, they may inadvertently introduce additional complexity that requires careful management to maintain code quality.

We examine the emergence of enstrophy in two-dimensional Euler flows, demonstrating that the squared vorticity gradient of a smooth solution to the Euler equation is not conserved along particle trajectories. This result stems from the inherent non-commutativity between the flow map and the curl operator. Furthermore, we establish a 2D Navier-Stokes analogue, showing that in the limit of vanishing viscosity, the flow map and the curl operator commute, leading to the conclusion that the flow map and the curl operator commute in the zero-viscosity limit, which implies enstrophy conservation along particle paths for the limiting solution. This study introduces a deep learning approach for classifying large-scale 3D point clouds, evaluated using a dataset of cuneiform tablets. The research addresses the challenge of limited labeled data by employing a hybrid strategy that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with data augmentation. The workflow begins by converting point clouds into images via the projection of their point clouds onto a 2D plane. These images are then processed by a CNN to extract features, which are subsequently classified using a support vector machine (SVM). The results demonstrate that this method achieves an accuracy of 98.8% on the test set. Furthermore, the integration of CNNs with SVMs yielded a 1.5% accuracy improvement over the standalone CNN model. The authors conclude that this approach is effective for classifying point clouds and holds significant potential for applications in archaeology and cultural heritage preservation.

The muon $g-2$ anomaly offers compelling evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model, potentially pointing to a massive spin-2 particle. This study examines the theoretical limits of such a framework, focusing on the specific scenario where a massive spin-2 particle is responsible for the muon $g-2$ discrepancy. We demonstrate that while a single spin-2 particle alone cannot account for the anomaly, it becomes viable when accompanied by additional new particles. Furthermore, we establish that the spin-2 field must possess a mass below 100 MeV, and the total new particle contribution to the anomaly cannot exceed 25% of the total.

This paper introduces a game-theoretic model of negotiation during political crises, where leaders must decide between a shared success outcome and a shared failure outcome. The analysis demonstrates that leaders' choices are driven by the need to appease their respective domestic groups. The model reveals that a greater number of domestic groups tends to foster more crisis compromises. These findings are consistent with observed trends in crisis evolution and align them with empirical evidence.

The ANTARAS neutrino observatory, situated in the Mediterranean Sea, has conducted online searches for correlated neutrino and gravitational wave (GW) signals since 2017. This review details the analysis methods and outcomes from the first GW alert dataset comprising 1,137 events from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, as well as a sample of 146 electromagnetic transient events from the Swift satellite. Additionally, ANTARAS data were cross-referenced with alerts from the Fermi-GBM and INTEGRAL satellites, covering 133 and 110 events, respectively. No significant correlations were identified between neutrino arrival times and GW or electromagnetic events. Consequently, the study establishes upper limits on the fraction of astrophysical sources producing neutrinos and GWs within the observed non-significant upper bounds.

High-contrast adaptive optics (AO) instruments are essential for exoplanet detection and characterization, yet they are susceptible to optical aberrations from the telescope's primary mirror. These aberrations, which can be induced by the primary support structure, degrade AO performance. This study utilizes ZEMAX to model a 10-meter class telescope and its AO system, evaluating the impact of primary mirror aberrations on the Strehl ratio (SR) and the contrast achieved by an AO system. The results indicate that the primary support structure can degrade the Strehl ratio by approximately 10% and lower the contrast by roughly 100 times. Consequently, the authors propose that the impact of primary support structure on the AO system be addressed in future telescope designs.

We introduce a novel, efficient, and precise density functional for periodic systems, designed to accurately predict phonon frequencies across a broad spectrum of materials. This approach integrates a computationally efficient, nonlocal exchange-correlation potential with a computationally efficient, nonlocal, and precise kinetic energy functional. This combination effectively corrects the errors inherent in the Kohn-Sham eigenvalues and bands, yielding reliable potential energy surfaces. Consequently, our method enables the accurate computation of phonon frequencies for diverse materials—including insulators, semiconductors, and metals—using standard computational techniques.

This paper examines forward Karp-Miller analysis within Petri nets, specifically addressing the conditions under which this method can be transformed into a version of WSTS-based analysis. The study focuses on two primary scenarios: those involving bounded Petri nets and those involving bounded input. For the former, we demonstrate that forward Karp-Miller analysis is equivalent to forward domain analysis using the specific domain constructed by Karp and Miller's original algorithm. For the latter, we establish that forward Karp-Miller analysis is equivalent to WSTS-based analysis when employing a particular quasi-ordering derived from the image finite property.

The Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) serves as the primary instrument on NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, operating within the 60 MeV to 300 GeV energy range. This paper details an application of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to enhance Fermi-LAT data. The study utilizes a dataset of 100,000 simulated sky maps, each containing 100,000 events, to train the CNN. The model was designed to classify events as either signal or background based on their spatial and energy characteristics. The trained network was subsequently applied to a genuine Fermi-LAT event sample, yielding a refined dataset. The resulting maps exhibit significantly improved sensitivity and a marked increase in the visibility of variable sources. The authors anticipate that these techniques will prove valuable for future investigations into the nature of the gamma-ray sky.

This work investigates the emergence of classicality within the quantum realm, specifically focusing on decoherence and the role of the environment. It demonstrates that environmental interaction is essential for the quantum-to-classical transition, as it selects preferred bases and specific states that appear classical. Furthermore, the study examines the philosophical implications of these findings, arguing that the classical limit is not an inherent property of the universe but rather an emergent one.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating the sum of two ellipsoids using the general geometric outer bound, a problem that extends to computing a geometric-level "n-way set union" operation. The proposed approach introduces a novel framework for identifying the maximal volume subset within a Minkowski sum of two ellipsoids. By leveraging this framework, we derive several generalization-based approximations for the union of n-way set unions involving multiple ellipsoids. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods through numerical experiments.

Tabular datasets are ubiquitous in real-world applications, yet their analysis remains difficult due to the intricate interplay between diverse row types and the heterogeneous mix of data types within columns. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework that integrates row attention mechanisms with contrastive pre-training. This approach enables the model to capture complex row-to-row dependencies and extract a comprehensive set of features that encapsulates both local and global data characteristics. We further introduce a new attention architecture designed to explicitly model relationships between different column types. Experimental results demonstrate that SAINT achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks across multiple domains, including fraud detection, credit scoring, and medical applications. Additionally, we show that the model learns robust representations through contrastive pre-training, yielding significant performance gains on downstream tabular tasks.

This paper presents a novel methodology for analyzing radio frequency (RF) deep learning transfer learning behavior, utilizing a dataset of synthetic radio signals. We specifically examine how the number of training channels impacts transfer learning within convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for signal classification. Our findings indicate that while the performance of CNNs trained on low channel counts degrades when exposed to data with higher channel counts, the reverse scenario yields improved performance. Additionally, the study reveals that the classification accuracy of a CNN is contingent upon the channel count utilized during its training.

Center vices are crucial for understanding the confinement mechanism in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). This study examines how the lattice-generated center vortex model aligns with the $SU(3)$ $\zeta$-Gribov modified Yang-Mills theory. We propose a new gauge-invariant quantity called the center region, which is defined as the center-valued link product within a minimal surface connecting a given link to its dual. This quantity effectively isolates the center vortex contribution from a specific link. Our analysis reveals that the center vortex model accurately reproduces the Gribov behavior observed in gauge-invariant observables, specifically the Polyakov loop and the center symmetry.

The Dark Energy Survey's Low Surface Brightness Galaxy (LSBG) sample is characterized by a low stellar mass, which makes them highly susceptible to dark matter annihilation signals. This study utilizes the Y3 release of DES to constrain dark matter annihilation cross-sections by analyzing the Y3 LSBG sample. We employ the same statistical framework as our prior work, which utilized the Y1 sample, to derive constraints on the annihilation cross-section. Our results indicate that the Y3 sample yields tighter constraints than Y1, with a 95% confidence level upper limit on the cross-section of $\sigma v < 1.1 \times 10^{-25} \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$ for a 10 GeV dark matter particle. This represents an improvement of 20% over the Y1 results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Y3 sample provides a 10% stronger constraint than the KiDS-1000 sample.

Software maintenance is a critical, time-intensive endeavor that often involves locating specific code fragments within large codebases. While prior research has explored various automated query reformulation strategies to assist maintainers, these methods typically depend on expensive, expert-annotated datasets that are difficult to acquire. To address this limitation, we introduce QUICKAR, a novel dataset constructed through crowdsourcing. In QUICKAR, software engineers are prompted to submit queries and subsequently provide alternative reformulations along with natural language descriptions of code element semantics. We evaluate our dataset's quality using a series of tests and demonstrate that QUICKAR significantly outperforms existing data-driven query reformulation approaches in locating code elements. Additionally, we present Q-RE, a new query reformulation model trained on QUICKAR, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results in code element search tasks.

This study introduces a novel finite element approach for solving the multi-compartmental Darcy equations, which model fluid flow through porous media containing distinct phases. The authors develop a parameter-robust preconditioner for the resulting linear systems, ensuring rapid convergence across varying permeabilities and reaction rates. Theoretical analysis provides the preconditioner's spectral equivalence, while numerical experiments confirm its efficiency.

This study introduces a new approach to the challenging task of abstractive dialogue summarization, aiming to create concise summaries that retain key information. We present a novel framework that restructures dialogue interactions by leveraging discourse relations to synthesize a summary. This method operates in two stages: first, it constructs discourse trees by identifying connections between dialogue turns, and subsequently, it generates summaries by reasoning over these trees. Notably, our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in a zero-shot setting, where it derives summaries for unseen dialogoes without prior training examples.

This study introduces a novel approach to predict Doppler broadening across various nuclear cross sections by employing a physically informed deep neural network (PINN). The methodology integrates Doppler broadening physics directly into the loss function, enabling the model to learn the underlying physical principles. The resulting predictions are benchmarked against standard tables generated by the NJOY code. The proposed method demonstrates exceptional accuracy, with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 0.01% for the thermal neutron fission cross section of $^{235}$U. Furthermore, the model exhibits robust generalization, successfully predicting Doppler broadening for other isotopes and energy ranges without retraining.

This work introduces the notion of $n$-pre-Lie algebras, a generalization of pre-Lie algebras that incorporates $n$-ary pre-Lie algebras as a specific instance. We define a notion of $n$-associativity for these algebras, demonstrating that $n$-associativity is equivalent to the condition that the $n$-associated $n$-pre-Lie algebra forms a $n$-Lie algebra. Furthermore, we examine the dendrification of $n$-ary pre-Lie algebras, proving that every dendritied $n$-ary pre-Lie algebra constitutes a double. As a corollary, we show that the dendrification of a pre-Lie algebra also satisfies the double structure property.

This study introduces a new framework for mixed quality of service (QoS) in cell-free massive MIMO systems, designed to accommodate users with diverse QoS requirements. The approach employs a single optimization objective to jointly determine user association, transmit power allocation, and data rates. The resulting problem is non-convex due to the interdependence of association and power variables alongside the concavity of achievable data rates. To address this, a two-phase iterative algorithm is proposed. The first phase utilizes a successive convex approximation method to solve for user association, power, and data rates, while the second phase applies a greedy strategy to derive a near-optimal integer solution for user association. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing solutions.

For any function $f$ within the class $C^1(\mathbb{T})$, this paper demonstrates that the sequence of translation operators defined by $T_{\varepsilon}f(x)=f(x+\varepsilon)$ converges uniformly with respect to $x$ as $\varepsilon$ approaches zero.

We investigate the interplay between shear-induced flow, structural organization, and memory in a sheared disordered system. By employing a model that links particle dynamics to a mesoscopic order parameter, we demonstrate that the system's response is governed by a competition between the applied shear and a self-interaction term. This term represents an effective shear resistance that drives a transition from a flowing to a jammed state. We further analyze the system's memory by contrasting the steady-state jammed response with its transient behavior immediately following a shear startup. We find that the jammed state is inherently more robust against the development of memory than the flowing state. Ultimately, our findings offer insights into the complex dynamics of sheared disordered materials, with potential relevance for understanding the rheology of biological tissues.

Object detection is a fundamental computer vision task with applications ranging from autonomous driving to medical imaging. In real-world scenarios, however, the environment is rarely static; instead, it undergoes continuous changes, necessitating the ability to learn incrementally from evolving data streams. This paper reviews continual object detection, a critical area focused on acquiring new knowledge without compromising previously acquired skills. We begin by defining key concepts and presenting a taxonomy of existing methods, followed by an analysis of specific techniques, their advantages, and limitations. Furthermore, we discuss the current challenges and future research directions in this domain.

The paper investigates the medium-modified gluon-to-charmonium splitting function within the BDMPS-Z framework. It derives the differential gluon-to-charmonium emission spectrum, which serves as the foundational building block for calculating jet-to-jet observables. By incorporating the non-Abelian Coulomb potential, the splitting function is modified to account for bound-state dynamics. Consequently, the resulting medium-modified spectrum exhibits a significant dependence on the non-Abelian potential, marking a distinct departure from the standard splitting function found in the DGLAP evolution framework.

Domain adaptation (DA) and domain generalization (DG) are two distinct strategies for addressing domain shifts in machine learning. While DA relies on the assumption that the target domain exists within the source domain's distribution, DG operates under the premise that the target domain lies outside the source distribution. Despite their differing foundations, both approaches aim to enhance model performance on target data. This study introduces a novel approach that integrates explainability into DG for image classification, leveraging shared representations between source and target domains to improve generalization. By utilizing self-supervised learning to extract these commonalities, the method employs Grad-CAM to generate heatmaps highlighting relevant features. These visualizations guide the selection of a subset of representative source domains, which are then used to train the model. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on DG tasks, surpassing existing methods by 1.5% to 2.5% in accuracy.
This paper outlines a blockchain-based framework designed to enhance security, knowledge sharing, and collaboration among agents operating within restricted domains of the Internet infrastructure.

$\alpha$-attractor models are a significant category of inflationary theories that encompass numerous well-known scenarios, such as chaotic, quadratic, and $E$-model inflations. This study examines the $\alpha$-attractor framework by analyzing the scalar spectral index ($n_s$) and the tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$), with a specific focus on the parameter $\alpha$. We demonstrate that the $\alpha$-attractor model is capable of describing a wide range of inflationary observations. Furthermore, we analyze the model's predictions for $n_s$ and $r$ across various values of $\alpha$, comparing these forecasts with the latest observational data. Our findings indicate that the $\alpha$-attractor model is consistent with current data when $\alpha$ is small, but becomes inconsistent when $\alpha$ is large.

End-to-end Artificial Intelligence (AI) pipelines encompass the entire workflow from data acquisition to model deployment, a process that is computationally intensive and demands significant resources. Optimizing these pipelines is essential for enhancing computational efficiency and reducing costs. This paper outlines strategies for optimizing end-to-end AI pipelines on Intel Xeon processors, covering data preprocessing, model training, and model inference. We examine various optimization techniques, including parallelization, vectorization, and hardware acceleration, and provide practical examples demonstrating how to apply these methods to optimize performance.

This paper introduces a semantic communication framework based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) and vector quantization (VQ). The system utilizes a shared encoder-decoder architecture, where the encoder transmits a quantized index of the message's latent representation, while the decoder reconstructs the message from this index. We evaluate the framework's performance using the mean squared error (MSE) as a fidelity metric and assess its robustness against channel noise. Furthermore, we examine the trade-off between compression ratio and MSE to determine the system's sensitivity to the bit allocation for the quantized index.

Data-driven analytics has become a cornerstone of modern society, with vast amounts of data collected daily from diverse sources. This data fuels critical decisions in fields ranging from healthcare and finance to transportation and education. However, the sheer volume, variety, and velocity of these data streams have created significant challenges for traditional analytics methods. Consequently, there is an urgent need for new paradigms that can efficiently process, analyze, and derive insights from such complex information. This paper introduces the concept of Interactive, Adaptive, and Result-aware Big Data Analytics (IAR-BDA), a comprehensive framework designed to handle big data analytics tasks. We begin by defining the fundamental principles of IAR-BDA and outlining its key characteristics. We then survey current Big Data analytics frameworks and examine how they align with IAR-BDA requirements. Finally, we identify critical open issues and outline potential future research directions in this evolving field.

Doctrines offer a unified framework for formalizing diverse mathematical theories, while modalities within these doctrines enable the abstraction of various forms of logic. This paper presents the comonadic lifting monad, which serves as a universal construction for modal operators in any doctrinal context. This approach generalizes earlier methods applicable to standard (fibrational) settings. We demonstrate that the doctrinal commutativity condition corresponds precisely to the preservation of preserved truth. Furthermore, we establish that the doctrinal comonad forms a bi-adjunction with the doctrinal lifting monad, a relationship that induces corresponding bi-adjunctions between the categories of structured and modalized doctrines.

The Network Autoregressive (NA) model is a prominent tool for analyzing time series data within network structures, yet it relies on the assumption of normally distributed errors, which often fails in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a Bayesian nonparametric graphical assistant grouped NA model that relaxes this normality constraint. The proposed approach employs a flexible nonparametric prior for error distributions and utilizes an innovative graphical assistant to efficiently estimate time-varying network effects. Simulation results demonstrate that this new model achieves superior performance compared to standard group NA specifications. Finally, the model's practical value is illustrated through the analysis of US state-level unemployment rates.

Validating scientific assertions necessitates the identification of supporting evidence within the corpus of scientific literature. However, most claims only require a small subset of the available context documents to be verified. This observation motivates our proposal of a streamlined methodology for evidence retrieval. We introduce a two-step process that first retrieves a compact, high-yield set of candidate documents and subsequently identifies specific sentence-level evidence from that selection to substantiate the claim. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach not only matches the performance of leading state-of-the-art models but also achieves these outcomes using 70% fewer parameters.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) serves as a non-invasive imaging technique capable of generating high-resolution, cross-sectional images of the eye's posterior segment. This modality is particularly valuable for diagnosing and monitoring various ocular diseases, including glaucoma, macular edema, and diabetic retinopathy. However, the manual interpretation of OCT scans is a time-consuming and laborious process. To address this, the current study proposes an automated method for segmenting the posterior eye segment and extracting its key anatomical structures. The methodology comprises two primary stages: first, a deep learning framework utilizing a U-Net architecture to delineate the boundaries of the posterior eye segment; second, the application of a graph-based algorithm to isolate specific structures within that region. The system's efficacy was validated using a dataset of 1,000 OCT scans from the Glaucoma Prognosis and Imaging (GPI) database. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a segmentation accuracy of 94.1% and an extraction accuracy of 90.1%.

Superstatistics serves as a statistical framework for analyzing systems characterized by fluctuating parameters, a concept that has been successfully applied to model fluctuating reaction times in cognitive psychology. This study introduces a neural superstatistics model designed to capture the fluctuating dynamics of cognition by employing a Bayesian approach. This method allows for the estimation of superstatistical parameters from behavioral data, effectively modeling how cognitive dynamics change over time. The model's utility is demonstrated by analyzing reaction times from a task involving the identification of vowels. The findings reveal that a superstatistical model provides a superior fit to the data compared to standard models, thereby offering a more accurate representation of the underlying cognitive processes.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for the explicit expansion of Mersenne primes. The approach integrates a revised Lucas theorem, a fresh concept regarding prime generating sequences, and the application of the binomial theorem.

This paper investigates hydrodynamic manifolds for kinetic equations, which are typically expressed as $f(t,x,v)$ and describe the evolution of particle distributions in phase space. We establish that these manifolds, which reduce the complex kinetic equations to simpler hydrodynamic forms, can be represented as power series in the Knudsen number $\epsilon$. Specifically, the manifold is defined by $f = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \epsilon^n f_n$. We demonstrate that these coefficients, $f_n$, decompose into two components: an exact hydrodynamic part, $f_n^h$, and an orthogonal residual, $R_n^h$. The exact component arises from the hydrodynamic equations, while the residual represents the higher-order corrections necessary for precision. We further prove that the residual term $R_n^h$ remains orthogonal to the hydrodynamic modes and decays rapidly, ensuring the stability of the manifold expansion. This decomposition provides a rigorous framework for deriving both exact and approximate hydrodynamic models from kinetic equations.

We present a novel method for quantifying the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies by utilizing the subthermally excited C I (1-0) line. This approach relies on the fact that the C I (1-0) line is subthermally excited in the cold molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies, meaning its intensity is highly sensitive to the density of the gas. We demonstrate that the ratio of C I (1-0) to CO (1-2) emission, denoted as $R_{C I}$, serves as a reliable indicator of the molecular gas reservoirs' coldness. This ratio is defined as $R_{C I} = \frac{I_{C I (1-0)}}{I_{CO (1-2)}}$, where $I$ represents the integrated intensity of the respective line. We show that $R_{C I}$ is a function of the molecular gas reservoirs' coldness, which is characterized by the ratio of the molecular gas reservoirs' coldness to the total gas reservoirs' coldness, denoted as $f_{cold}$. This ratio is defined as $f_{cold} = \frac{I_{CO (1-2)}}{I_{CO (1-2)} + I_{CO (2-1)}}$. We demonstrate that $R_{C I}$ is a function of the molecular gas reservoirs' coldness, which is characterized by the ratio of the molecular gas

This paper introduces the inaugural treebank of Spoken Frisian-Dutch code-switching, which was gathered from a corpus of interviews. The dataset encompasses 120,000 words across 10 interviews, featuring a mix of Frisian-Dutch combinations. It includes annotations for both languages, with specific attention to the identification and tagging of code-switches. The authors detail the methods used to annotate the data and provide an analysis of the linguistic characteristics of Frisian-Dutch mixing. Additionally, they evaluate the linguistic balance between the two languages and examine the distribution of switched segments within different parts of speech.

This study investigates the impact of stellar mass on the photoevaporation of protoplanetary discs, utilizing a sample of 100 T Tauri stars with masses ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 solar masses. We employ the photoevaporation model developed by \citet{2014ApJ...786..131H}, which incorporates the stellar mass–age relation derived by \citet{2014ApJ...784..100H}. Our results indicate that the mass dependence of photoevaporation rates is significant, particularly for low-mass stars. Specifically, the rate of mass loss is approximately 100 times higher for a 0.1 solar mass star compared to a 0.5 solar mass star at an age of 10 million years. Consequently, the evolution of disc structure and mass loss varies substantially with stellar mass. Furthermore, the inner disc of a 0.1 solar mass star is more susceptible to photoevaporation than its outer regions, whereas in more massive stars, the outer disc evaporates faster. We also demonstrate that the inner disc of a 0.1 solar mass star transitions to a gas-free state much earlier than in higher-mass stars. Finally, we argue that the observed discrepancy between the predicted and actual disc mass distributions for low-mass stars suggests that mechanisms other than photoevaporation, such as radial drift, must also contribute to disc mass

This study introduces a family of high-order, explicit time integration schemes designed specifically for structural dynamics within the isogeometric framework. These methods are tailored for linear elastic problems and utilize the generalized-$\alpha$ approach to mitigate numerical oscillations. The proposed techniques are optimal, meaning they reach the highest order of accuracy permitted by the constraints on the number of evaluation points per time step. Furthermore, the methods are fully explicit, requiring no iterative solution of linear systems. A key advantage is that the only problem-specific constant needed is the spatial discretization matrix, which can be computed once and reused for all time steps. The paper provides a detailed derivation of these methods, along with a comprehensive numerical validation using a beam element to demonstrate their efficacy.

This study investigates the dynamics of a polaron within a one-dimensional double-well, specifically focusing on the decay of the polaronic residue caused by the scattering of excitons. We demonstrate that both interband and intraband excitons can induce polarmion residue decay, with interband excitons driving the initial decay stage and intraband excitons governing the later stage. Furthermore, we analyze the effects of the polarmion's position on the double-well center and the momentum of the resulting excitons, alongside an examination of the influence of the polarmion-Bose coupling strength on the decay rates.

This study introduces a multi-stage stochastic programming framework designed to optimize logistics planning for disaster relief operations. The model's primary objective is to minimize the aggregate costs of relief supplies, which include transportation, inventory holding, and unmet demand. The stochastic elements encompass the timing of disaster onset, the spatial distribution of affected areas, and the specific requirements of victims. The model incorporates specific constraints to ensure that storage capacities at distribution centers are respected and that the number of available vehicles is not exceeded. To solve this model, we developed a specialized solution methodology that integrates a tailored Benders decomposition approach with a tailored scenario tree generation algorithm. The study further analyzes the computational performance of this method and evaluates how its efficiency varies based on the number of scenarios in the tree and the number of decision stages.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are currently detecting the stochastic gravitational wave background (GWB) generated by supermassive black hole binaries. However, the GWB's signal is likely contaminated by contributions from inspiralling binaries within the Milky Way. This study introduces a PTAs-specific post-Newtonian (PN) waveform model for these inspiralling binaries, which incorporates orbital eccentricity and extends accuracy up to 2.5PN order. We demonstrate that this waveform model is sufficiently precise to forecast PTAs signals for inspiralling binaries with orbital periods exceeding 10 years. Furthermore, we evaluate the computational efficiency of the waveform model and its associated parameter estimation pipeline. The results indicate that the waveform model is computationally efficient, with a single evaluation requiring approximately 0.01 seconds.

This study examines how agents' individual decisions are influenced by the aggregate behavior of others, a framework known as the global game. In this setup, each agent receives a private signal and a common public signal, and must select a binary action. Agents derive utility primarily from their own action choice, with a secondary component driven by the aggregate actions of the group. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the public signal reveals the proportion of agents who chose action 1, a proportion we term the "observed actions." These observed actions are shown to be informative regarding the true fundamentals of the game. Furthermore, we establish that the public signal functions as a sufficient statistic for these observed actions, enabling agents to update their private beliefs and make more informed choices. We also identify scenarios where this informational value is amplified, leading to a higher fraction of agents choosing action 1. Finally, we illustrate the practical relevance of our findings through an application to the Bitcoin network.

This study presents a method for characterizing high-loss liquids within the 750 GHz to 1100 GHz frequency range, utilizing on-chip coplanar waveguides (CPW) integrated with a liquid sample. The proposed technique is demonstrated by measuring the dielectric properties of ethylene glycol and water. A key advantage of this method is its ability to achieve a high electric field strength in the sample, which is essential for studying phenomena occurring under high-voltage conditions.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant global disruption, necessitating the implementation of various countermeasures to mitigate its impact. This paper introduces a novel framework, AIRSENSE-TO-ACT, designed to assist in formulating these strategies. The system integrates data from diverse sources, including air quality metrics, meteorological conditions, and weather forecasts, to analyze the transmission dynamics of SARS-CoV-2. By employing machine learning algorithms, it identifies patterns in how environmental factors influence the spread of the virus. The study further outlines the system's capabilities for processing and visualizing data, and discusses its potential applications in guiding public health interventions.

This paper introduces a novel, multi-resolution SPH framework designed to address multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. The approach utilizes a single set of SPH equations where the partition function is defined by a multi-resolution kernel, composed of sub-kernels with varying support and resolution. This kernel structure enables the model to differentiate between fluid inputs based on their strength of interaction with a solid boundary. Specifically, the kernel is engineered to strongly couple a primary phase with the solid while simultaneously weakly coupling a secondary phase. The model's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations involving two immiscible fluids interacting with a moving rigid body, including cases where a buoyant droplet rises to impact a solid surface.

Nodal lines within momentum space are recognized as one-dimensional topological defects, where Hamiltonian eigenvalues cross and coalesce. These structures are safeguarded by nontrivial topological indices defined on a surrounding torus. This review examines the topological characteristics of such nodal lines, with a particular focus on recent experimental demonstrations across photonic systems and other platforms.

This document presents the results from the collaboration between the Event Generator (EG) working group and the HL-LHC Computing Review Stage-2 Event Generator group. It examines the specific software necessities for simulating events at future collider facilities and outlines potential applications for the HL-LHC environment. The report further details the anticipated computational demands and identifies the primary obstacles to implementation.

This article demonstrates an invariance property regarding certain partial means derived from a specific subset of a vector space to its full set. These means include examples such as the Axler, Foster, and Schaefer partial geometric and harmonic means.

We present a novel study of the outer Galaxy's dark molecular gas, utilizing the 12CO J=1-0 line data from the Galactic Legacy All-Sky Survey (GLASS). Our analysis reveals that the 12CO emission intensity remains significant out to approximately 15 kpc from the Galactic center, with a peak intensity of 1.5 K km s$^{-1}$ at a distance of 10.5 kpc. The intensity profile exhibits a double-peaked structure, with maxima located at 10.5 kpc and 15.5 kpc. Additionally, the velocity dispersion increases with distance from the center, rising from 1.5 km s$^{-1}$ at 10.5 kpc to 2.5 km s$^{-1}$ at 15.5 kpc. These findings indicate that the outer Galaxy's molecular gas is distributed in a thick disk, with a scale height of 1.5 kpc. We propose that this thick disk is composed of molecular gas that has been heated by supernovae and stellar winds, resulting in a velocity dispersion of 1.5 km s$^{-1}$ at 10.5 kpc and 2.5 km s$^{-1}$ at 15.5 kpc.

This study examines a closed economy featuring a single firm and a continuum of workers, where firm profits are distributed among workers via shares denoted by $\alpha$. The analysis determines the equilibrium outcomes of the resulting wage and profit-sharing strategies. It demonstrates that the equilibrium wage and profit share are uniquely determined, with wages increasing in response to higher productivity. Furthermore, the paper establishes that the equilibrium profit share remains constant over time, provided the productivity distribution does not shift.

This study investigates collective dynamics within disordered polar active matter systems, specifically focusing on conditions of high density where interactions are dominated by steric constraints. We demonstrate that, in the absence of any alignment interactions, these systems exhibit a distinct dynamical transition. This transition is defined by a shift from a disordered state to a dynamic phase characterized by large-scale motion, occurring at a critical value of the active force. We establish that this phenomenon arises from a competition between the alignment forces generated by active motion and steric constraints. Furthermore, we identify a specific parameter regime where active forces dominate, leading to a dynamic phase that displays long-range order.

Semileptonic transitions involving double charmed baryons are investigated here using the bag model. The study focuses on the semileptonic decay of the $\Xi_{cc}^{++}$ baryon into the $\Omega_c^0$, $\Sigma_c^0$, and $\Sigma_c^+$ states. Within the framework of the Standard Model, the decay rates and form factors for these processes are determined.

This study introduces a novel task called localization from embodied dialog, which involves reconstructing an environment's layout and an agent's position based solely on natural language descriptions of the dialogue. This work addresses a significant gap in existing embodied AI research, which typically relies on localization from visual inputs or assumes prior knowledge of the environment's layout. By leveraging the unique ability of language to articulate spatial relationships, our approach aims to enhance the generalization capabilities of AI systems. We developed a dataset featuring diverse indoor scenes and generated dialogues using a dialogue model. Our findings indicate that even with a restricted vocabulary of directional terms, the model can effectively localize the agent within the environment.

This paper introduces a new methodology for automatically selecting frequency bands in vibration analysis, designed to enhance the effectiveness of machine learning techniques for fault diagnosis in rotating equipment. The approach involves calculating a Band Relevance Factor (BRF) for each frequency band, which is subsequently used to determine the optimal frequency bands for diagnosis. The proposed method was validated using a dataset from a bearing test rig, demonstrating its ability to accurately identify fault types. The results indicate that the new frequency band selection method yields superior performance compared to existing techniques.

We report muon-spin relaxation and rotation studies on the noncentrosymmetric superconductors CaIrSi$_3$ and CaPtSi$_3$, which exhibit bulk superconducting transitions at $T_c = 1.6$ K and $T_c = 1.4$ K, respectively. The observed muon-spin relaxation rates for both materials are consistent with a fully gapped, three-dimensional superconducting state. Furthermore, the absence of a detectable spin precession frequency suggests that the superconducting order parameter possesses either a small energy gap or a low-muon-spin-polarization relaxation rate.

This study introduces a novel approach to mitigate the curse of dimensionality in nonlinear optimal feedback control for stochastic systems. The strategy involves discretizing the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation using sparse grids, which subsequently allows for the reconstruction of the optimal control law via a sparse grid spectral method. The paper details the theoretical foundations of this discretization scheme, analyzes the convergence behavior of the resulting approximate solutions, and demonstrates the method's application through two case studies: a linear quadratic regulator and a portfolio optimization problem.

We present a classification framework for multi-outcome quantum measurements implemented on qudits, the quantum system's fundamental unit with dimension $d$. Our methodology relies on the measurement's probability distribution, represented as a $d$-dimensional vector, alongside a specific cost function that quantifies the distance between two such probability distributions. We demonstrate that the cost function can be formulated as a matrix element of a unitary operator acting on a $2d$-dimensional Hilbert space. This formulation enables the cost function to be expressed as a sum of terms, each corresponding to an entangled two-qudit state. Consequently, the task of minimizing this cost function can be addressed using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) protocol. We illustrate the practical application of this method by demonstrating its use in calculating the Wasserstein distance between two probability distributions.

This study introduces a novel framework for analyzing and managing multi-energy dynamical systems, which are pivotal for decarbonization efforts. We formulate these systems as differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) and derive their associated state-space representation. We then develop a new control architecture designed to optimize the collective behavior of these multi-energy systems, utilizing the proposed state-space model to evaluate the impact of external control signals on system dynamics. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through a case study on a multi-energy system, demonstrating its potential to enhance the operational efficiency of future low-carbon infrastructure.

We investigate the two-dimensional bond percolation model on square lattices using machine learning techniques. By training a neural network on configurations of small lattices, the network learns to identify the critical percolation threshold and predict local properties of the system. Leveraging this trained model, the study examines how percolation evolves as the lattice size approaches infinity. The findings reveal that the probability of a site belonging to a cluster of a specific finite size follows a scaling law, the exponents of which the network accurately determines. Furthermore, the analysis of the largest cluster distribution indicates that the network can also recover the parameters of the scaling law governing this distribution.

This study introduces a novel approach to simultaneously measure temperature and gas concentration within a fixed bed reactor using rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). By employing a specific pulse sequence, the method captures the thermal and concentration distribution of a nitrogen flow passing through a packed bed of stainless steel spheres. The system's temperature sensitivity is enhanced by applying a cryogenic precooling process to the probe, enabling the detection of temperature variations as minute as 0.1 K. The acquired data reveals the intricate relationship between temperature and concentration gradients, alongside the detailed thermal and concentration evolution of the gas flowing through the bed. Furthermore, the results indicate that the probe's precooling process is critical for achieving high thermal sensitivity in gas-solid systems. The findings offer valuable insights into the thermal behavior of such reactors, supporting the development of more efficient designs.

We introduce a phenomenological framework for superconductivity featuring quenched disorder and thermal fluctuations, which generates a reentrant superconducting phase. This model effectively captures the anomalous upper critical field behavior and the reentrant characteristics observed in UTe$_2$'s superconducting transition. We demonstrate that reentrant superconductivity can emerge in a second-order phase transition system containing a single order parameter, provided a second-order phase transition is accompanied by a change in symmetry. Furthermore, we illustrate that reentrant superconductivity can occur in a first-order phase transition without one, provided a second-order phase transition is accompanied by a change in symmetry. Ultra-wideband (UWB) technology is a leading candidate for next-generation wireless short-range communication, offering high data rates and precise localization. However, its performance is highly sensitive to environmental conditions, which can cause significant fluctuations in throughput. To address this, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework designed to automatically optimize Unshielded Pulse Modulation (UPM) parameters at runtime. This approach dynamically adjusts PHY layer configurations to maximize throughput by learning from the environment's channel state information. We demonstrate that our DRL-based PHY adaptation strategy outperforms traditional heuristic methods, achieving up to a 1.5-fold increase in data rates.

This paper examines the k-median clustering problem within the context of discrete Fr\'{e}ch\'{e}t and Hausdorff distances for polygonal curves. We demonstrate that the k-median problem under Fr\'{e}ch\'{e}t distance is NP-hard, whereas it admits a polynomial-time solution for the k-median problem under Hausdorff distance.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has emerged as a vital field for addressing complex, real-world issues, yet it faces significant hurdles, including the curse of dimensionality, non-stationarity, and the non-concave nature of the underlying optimization problem. This study introduces a novel MARL framework that models the task as a non-concave min-max optimization problem. We propose a min-max game featuring a non-convex primal component and a concave dual component, solved using a recently developed, simple, and efficient double-averaging primal-dual algorithm. Theoretical analysis confirms that the proposed method achieves an optimal convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the dual variable and $\mathcal{O}(\log T / \sqrt{T})$ for the primal variable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method's convergence rate is independent of the number of agents, thereby mitigating the curse of dimensionality. Extensive experiments on the StarCraft II benchmark validate the method's efficacy, showing that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

The coalgebraic $\mu$-calculus serves as a generalization of the standard $\mu$-calculus, where transition systems are replaced by sets equipped with a specified signature. This framework allows the formalization of various model checking variants, including those based on labeled transition systems, Kripke structures, and general transition systems. This paper presents a satisfiability checking method for the coalgebraic $\mu$-calculus that extends existing algorithms for the standard variant. Our approach targets monodic, finitary, and finitely supported coalgebras defined over a base signature. We demonstrate the method's applicability by extending existing algorithms to handle three specific instances: standard transition systems, labeled transition systems, and Kripke structures.

This study introduces a low-rank tensor approach for recovering sparse initial states in PDEs, utilizing Isogeometric Analysis (IGA) to formulate the governing equations. By leveraging the inherent low-rank structure of IGA, we establish a precise and efficient numerical framework. Specifically, we employ the tensor train format to represent the initial state's IGA coefficients, alongside the t-SVD singular value decomposition to iteratively refine the solution. This methodology is applied to both linear and nonlinear PDEs, with numerical results demonstrating the algorithm's efficiency and accuracy.

This study introduces a drive-by sensing approach for generating dense maps of air quality. The proposed method utilizes a facility location algorithm to identify optimal driving routes for data collection, followed by a deep learning model trained on these collected samples to predict air quality across the entire area. The model's accuracy is validated through field tests conducted in the city of Los Angeles. The resulting prediction maps are then compared against the Los Angeles Air Now system to assess performance. The findings demonstrate that the proposed drive-by sensing method is both effective and cost-efficient for creating high-density air quality maps.

This paper presents a novel, natural class of involutions on the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, denoted as the "second class," and applies them to the linear group defined over the truncated polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}[x]/(x^4)$. We construct the Weil representation for a general linear group under this inductive structure, and we demonstrate that the Weil involution acting on the resulting space is equivalent to an involution derived from the second-class framework.

Persuasive media, which includes advertisements, news, and entertainment, is designed to influence audience attitudes and behaviors toward specific subjects. The field of persuasive video generation (PGV) has attracted significant attention from researchers and practitioners alike, driven by the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). These technologies have enabled the automation of various persuasive video components, such as content analysis, storyboarding, and video synthesis. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of AI-driven PGV, examining its applications, challenges, and future trajectories. We begin by defining the core concepts of persuasion and reviewing the primary persuasive strategies employed in video generation. Subsequently, we analyze the diverse applications of PGV, ranging from marketing and advertising to education and entertainment. A central focus of this work is a systematic review of existing PGV approaches, categorized by their underlying tasks, including content understanding, video generation, and persuasive presentation. Finally, we discuss the current limitations of current methods and outline potential future research directions.

This study examines the quantum behavior of ions within quadrupole and octupole ion traps, specifically focusing on the ground state and the coherency between classical and quantum mechanics. The analysis reveals that the ground state of a trapped ion corresponds to squeezed vacuum, whereas a coherently oscillating ion aligns with squeezed coherent states of motion. These states are fully described by their characteristic functions, which are derived by solving the Fokker-Planck equation. The resulting analysis of these states' properties indicates that the specific parameters of the ion trap can be precisely controlled to generate the desired states of motion.

Neuroscience models are frequently optimized using data-driven methods, a process that often necessitates extensive computational resources. Consequently, the need to explore vast parameter spaces has become increasingly critical, particularly for large-scale models. This paper introduces a novel approach to navigating these expansive hyper-parameter spaces by employing meta-learning techniques. We demonstrate that meta-learning can effectively guide the selection of hyper-parameters for the Hodgkin-Haxey model, a foundational unit in neuroscience. By utilizing a specific dataset, we identify optimal hyper-parameters that minimize the error between model outputs and experimental data. Furthermore, we apply our proposed meta-learning framework to the task of learning to optimize hyper-parameters across multiple datasets. Our findings indicate that this approach enables the efficient discovery of high-performing hyper-parameters for new datasets by leveraging insights from previously analyzed sets.

Camouflaged object segmentation (COTS) is a difficult task in computer vision that involves isolating objects that are easily confused with their surroundings. While existing methods have shown promise, they often struggle with the lack of diverse real-world data and the absence of standardized evaluation protocols. To address these issues, we introduce the Camouflaged Instance Segmentation IN-Wild (CIS-IW) dataset, which features a wide variety of scenarios and includes over 10,000 annotated images. We further establish a comprehensive benchmark suite to facilitate rigorous performance comparisons. Our findings indicate that current state-of-the-art models fail to meet the requirements of CIS-IW. Consequently, we propose a novel method that integrates multi-scale feature fusion with a dual-branch architecture to enhance the segmentation of camouflaged instances. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance on the proposed benchmark. The dataset and associated code are accessible at https://github.com/zhengqinxing/CIS-IW.

This study examines the consequences of Lorentz violation on superconductivity, specifically within the Ginzburg-Landau framework. The analysis reveals that Lorentz violation induces anisotropy in the superconducting state, manifesting as directional dependence in the superfluid density, coherence length, and penetration depth. Furthermore, the energy gap becomes complex, potentially leading to the emergence of spontaneous currents.

AI systems are increasingly integrated into critical decision-making processes, yet their inherent complexity and opacity make identifying and correcting errors difficult. This study introduces a novel crowdsourcing methodology designed to detect and verify AI mistakes, specifically targeting instances where human feedback is ignored. We tested this approach on a real-world application: a machine learning model for detecting COVID-19 from chest X-rays. By recruiting 1,000 participants to submit failure reports, we identified 1,034 errors, which were subsequently validated using an automated pipeline. Our analysis revealed that 81.4% of these validated errors involved cases where a model confidently predicted the wrong outcome. Furthermore, we examined how the diversity of error types and the frequency of error reporting varied across different participant demographics. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that deploying a crowdsourcing strategy for error identification and verification is both feasible and effective.

This paper introduces a novel, randomized decision routing (R(Det)^2) architecture designed for object detection, which integrates the strengths of two prominent approaches: region-based and anchor-based detectors. By leveraging region proposals, R(Det)^2 generates a limited set of high-quality candidate boxes, mirroring the efficiency of region detectors. Simultaneously, it employs on-box regression techniques to refine these proposals, matching the precision found in anchor-based systems. The method's flexibility allows it to adapt to various backbone networks and detection strategies, such as single-stage or two-stage frameworks. Extensive testing across multiple datasets—including MS COCO, Pascal VOC, Pascal-Context, and CityPersons—demonstrates that R(Det)^2 achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art detectors. Furthermore, the authors provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of the method's properties and its impact on detection accuracy.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which involve creating inputs that are nearly indistinguishable from originals yet cause the model to produce erroneous outputs. While Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) is a prominent adversarial technique, it is widely used in adversarial training to enhance DNN robustness. However, we demonstrate that adversarial training using FGSM induces catastrophic overfitting, characterized by the model's ability to correctly classify clean data but fail significantly on perturbed inputs. This phenomenon stems from the model learning to over-rely on specific input features that are easily disrupted by adversarial noise. To address this, we introduce ZeroGrad, a novel regularization method that penalizes gradients with respect to input features, thereby preventing the model from assigning excessive importance to any single feature. Our approach effectively mitigates catastrophic overfitting and improves robustness against FGSM attacks. Additionally, we utilize the ZeroGrad loss to elucidate the model's decision-making process, revealing that the model assigns higher significance to features that exhibit lower gradients.

This study examines the Thakurta metric, a proposed solution to Einstein's equations for a cosmological black hole, and argues that it fails to meet the criteria of a valid solution due to its violation of the energy conditions. Consequently, the Thakurta metric is not a physically viable representation of such an object. Furthermore, we demonstrate that astrophysical constraints derived by Bhattacharya et al. [1] regarding primordial black holes (PBPs) from Thakurta's analysis remain unaffected by this theoretical proposal.

This paper investigates the impact of persistent asset switching on a specific class of optimization algorithms inspired by hybrid systems, which are frequently utilized in financial portfolio management. These algorithms operate by alternating between a continuous-time, linear, feedback-driven control system and a discrete-time, linear, feedback-driven optimization routine. We demonstrate that the algorithm's stability is compromised when the switching frequency is high, yet we also establish sufficient conditions on the switching signal that ensure global convergence of asset prices to a unique, stable equilibrium point.

Bootstrapping represents a critical challenge in fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), a field that enables arbitrary computations on encrypted data. This paper introduces BTS, a novel bootstrapping mechanism designed to enhance the efficiency of the BGV encryption scheme. BTS leverages the inherent homomorphic properties of the scheme to perform modulus switching and relinearization, thereby reducing the computational overhead associated with these operations. Our experimental results indicate that BTS achieves a 1.7x speedup over the conventional approach for the BGV cryptosystem.

This paper investigates a random matrix ensemble featuring a logarithmic confining potential, $V(z) = \ln|z|^2 + \ln|z|$. While such logarithmic confining potentials are prevalent in various areas of physics, they typically resist exact solution. We demonstrate that this specific case is an exception, being fully solvable. We derive the partition function, eigenvalue correlation functions, and the joint eigenvalue probability density function (JPD). Additionally, we examine the large-$N$ asymptotic behavior of the model, showing that the eigenvalue density follows a Wigner semicircle law. We also analyze the model's behavior in the finite-$N$ regime.

This study experimentally examines quantum correlations within a two-qutrit spin system using a pair of quantum dots embedded in semiconductor heterostructures. We introduce a method for measuring correlations in a three-level system by decomposing the qutrit state into two superimposed qubit states. By analyzing the concurrence of these constituent qubit states, we determine the presence of both entanglement and intra-class correlations in the original two-qutrit system. Our findings demonstrate that the observed entanglement matches those reported in previous two-qutrit experiments, alongside the detection of intra-class entanglement between the qutrits. Furthermore, we observe that the system's entanglement remains robust against decoherence, maintaining functionality at temperatures as high as 1.2 K.

We introduce a framework for modeling correlations within multipartite systems that integrates the principles of locality with a specific constraint of "chain connectivity." This approach imposes limits on how local hidden variable models can represent correlations, thereby permitting such models to exist for only certain configurations. Our methodology relies on decomposing the set of all possible arrangements into equivalence classes defined by local symmetries; these classes are then organized into a hierarchical structure. Within this hierarchy, correlations for any given arrangement can be expressed as a linear combination of correlations associated with a minimal arrangement. This minimal structure is characterized by a chain of subsystems where each element interacts with its immediate neighbors. Consequently, we demonstrate that any local model accounting for these minimal correlations can be reformulated as a linear combination of models that factorize across the specified hierarchical chain. This factorization property is significant because it allows for the derivation of nontrivial inequalities that are violated by quantum mechanics.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a novel approach for generating continuous video streams. Our method leverages a pre-trained StyleGAN2 architecture, extending it with two new components: a generator that accepts noise as continuous temporal input, and a time-encoding module that transforms time into a feature vector. This design enables the synthesis of high-fidelity videos at any resolution, with the capability to produce unlimited video clips of identical content. Furthermore, our approach allows for the generation of content at specific timestamps, facilitating the creation of time-lapse sequences and enabling seamless video editing. Our findings demonstrate that StyleGAN-V effectively handles continuous video synthesis, outperforming existing methods in both quality and diversity.

The text outlines a method for calculating the rank difference of two elliptic curves linked by an epsilon correspondence. This approach provides an elementary demonstration of the finiteness of Selmer groups associated with admissible pairs of elliptic curves.

Accurate estimation of exposure dates is critical for forensic applications of thermoluminescence (TL) dating. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to automatically determine these dates by analyzing TL glow curves from the "ForensiK" TL system. The proposed method utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract a high-dimensional feature vector from the glow curve, which a subsequent regression model then uses to predict the date. This architecture was trained and validated on a dataset of 1,000 glow curves derived from 100 distinct samples. The results demonstrate that the deep learning approach significantly outperforms the conventional method, which relies on manually selected characteristic points. The automated system achieves a standard error of 10.2 days, compared to 19.3 days for the manual approach. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against variations in TL reader settings, such as heating rates and detector sensitivity, and maintains high accuracy even with noisy data.

This paper examines a category of double phase problems characterized by a singular term, defined within a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold that utilizes a specific completion of the Sobolev-Orlicz space. Our analysis incorporates the notion of a generalized Hardy potential, subject to a constraint on the summation of two distinct exponents.

The Fastcat simulator, developed by the University of Manchester, offers a comprehensive and flexible platform for modeling cone beam CT (CBCT) systems across both kV and MV energy ranges. This study evaluates the simulator's performance by comparing its outputs against measurements from a physical CBCT setup. The system under test utilizes a 320-slice CT scanner (Aquilion One, Toshiba) adapted for MV imaging with a custom-built, high-Z, high-density, and high-attenuation cone beam detector. To validate the kV and MV simulations, a phantom containing a 10 cm diameter sphere filled with a uniform mixture of water and iodine was employed. The phantom was rotated on a turntable to capture projections at 0.5° intervals. For the kV assessment, a 120 kV spectrum was used, while the MV assessment utilized a 3 MeV spectrum. Image reconstruction was performed using the FDK algorithm. Validation involved comparing simulated and experimental images across three metrics: image quality, HU accuracy, and scatter fraction. Results indicated that Fastcat accurately replicates the system's imaging characteristics, including scatter fraction and image quality. Additionally, the simulator's ability to model the MV detector's response was verified. Ultimately, Fastcat is confirmed as a robust and accurate tool for simulating CBCT systems.

Machine learning models are increasingly ubiquitous in daily life, yet their lack of transparency often hinders human comprehension. While recent efforts have focused on explainable AI (XAI) to address this, existing methods frequently fail to account for the inherent instability of explanations. This paper introduces a novel algorithm, Stabilized-LIME (S-LIME), designed to generate consistent LIME explanations. By leveraging the inherent instability identified in LIME models, our approach employs a two-stage process: first, it clusters similar instances to create representative points, and second, it aggregates the LIME explanations generated for these representatives to produce a stable final explanation. We validate S-LIME across various datasets and models, demonstrating that it achieves significantly more stable explanations than current state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a Bayesian framework designed to enhance the classification performance of machine learning models by leveraging explanation feedback. The approach is particularly valuable when such feedback is provided by human experts, as it allows the model to correct its own classification errors. We present a general method for updating classification probabilities that incorporates this feedback, while also introducing a specific variant for scenarios where explanation feedback is abundant. This variation enables the model to refine its predictions for instances with multiple potential explanations. The proposed framework is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its capacity to boost the accuracy of various classification algorithms when explanation feedback is utilized.

We investigate the evolution of $C^{2}$, strictly convex, mean curvature-constrained powers flow on the unit sphere. Our analysis demonstrates that every such flow converges to either a spherical shell or a half-space.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in image classification, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. This study investigates the frequency-domain characteristics of CNNs by introducing a novel Convolutional Neural Network in the Frequency Domain (CNNFD). This framework learns to map images directly to the frequency domain, where convolutional operations are executed via efficient point-wise multiplications. We demonstrate that CNNFDs exhibit superior performance compared to their spatial-domain counterparts across various datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Furthermore, we present evidence that the weights within CNNFDs encode meaningful information, suggesting that the frequency-domain approach offers both interpretability and enhanced efficiency.

Unsupervised image clustering is a fundamental task in computer vision, with deep learning approaches currently dominating the field. However, these methods often struggle with the high computational cost of training deep networks and frequently yield suboptimal results due to the instability of single clustering strategies. To address these issues, we introduce DeepCluE, a multi-layer ensemble framework designed to aggregate outputs from various clustering algorithms within a deep neural network. This approach leverages the deep network to extract high-level features and employs an ensemble mechanism to combine outputs from multiple layers, thereby enhancing overall clustering performance. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply multi-layer ensembles for clustering within deep learning contexts. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that DeepCluE significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving improvements of up to 10.3% and 10.1% in clustering accuracy, respectively.

This paper introduces a new framework designed to detect risks for financial institutions by leveraging a knowledge graph and automated news profiling. The system ingests and analyzes news articles to pinpoint relevant risk factors, subsequently constructing a knowledge graph that maps relationships between risk events and risk factors. This graph facilitates the generation of a risk network, which is subsequently used to identify and evaluate potential risk propagation pathways. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study of a specific bank, where it is used to pinpoint risk factors and build a knowledge graph that elucidates inter-risk factor connections. This graph is then leveraged to construct a risk network, which is used to identify and evaluate potential risk propagation pathways. This study introduces a novel approach to classification leveraging Topological Data Analysis (TDA). The method utilizes the persistent homology of simplicial complexes derived from a dataset to evaluate topological characteristics. We present a new distance metric to quantify the dissimilarity between two point sets based on their corresponding persistent diagrams. Additionally, we apply this distance metric to solve a binary classification task. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach yields competitive performance compared to other methods.

This paper introduces the concept of a "characterization," which refers to a specific collection of matrices capable of generating any given matrix through linear combinations.
